title: Martin Rispens & Son v. Hall Farms, Inc.
lead: Watermelon disease led a farm to sue its seed retailer and grower. The Indiana Supreme Court preserved particular warranty disputes and assent questions but directed judgment on tort claims under the then-governing product-liability and economic-loss rules.

actors.name: Hall Farms
actors.role: Knox County watermelon grower claiming crop losses

actors.name: Martin Rispens & Son
actors.role: Seed retailer asserting disclaimers and a price cap

actors.name: Petoseed
actors.role: Seed grower supplying the pertinent lots

actors.name: Richard Latin
actors.role: Purdue plant pathologist investigating the disease

proceedings: The trial court denied summary judgment; an interlocutory appellate ruling limited surviving claims. On transfer, the Indiana Supreme Court vacated that opinion and directed judgment on all claims except express warranties against both defendants and merchantability against Rispens.
limits: The surviving warranties were not found breached and no damages were awarded. The court did not decide tort applicability of contractual caps, authentication disputes, or unraised transfer issues. Its strict-liability and privity analysis addressed historical Indiana law.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Seedlings grew before disease devastated the fruit
sections.cue: Trace the purchase and emerging problem.
paragraphs: Hall Farms operated about 1,400 acres in Knox County and had successfully planted Prince Charles watermelon seed since 1982 or 1983. In August 1988 it ordered forty pounds from retailer Martin Rispens & Son at $85.40 per pound. Sealed one-pound cans arrived in February 1989. Petoseed grew the relevant lots in China and Mexico.

The farm germinated them in greenhouses in April. About fifteen seedlings developed yellow lesions April 25. Purdue pathologist Richard Latin ruled out the initially suspected gummy stem blight and fungus. The lesions did not stop growth or kill plants, and asymptomatic seedlings went into fields in early May.

A purple blotch appeared on a melon in early July, spread rapidly by midmonth, and ruined much of the crop by harvest. Most damaged fruit was plowed under in September. Volunteer plants the next summer were destroyed before Latin could inspect them; no fruit blotch appeared in 1990, including previously affected fields. Relying on his view that bacteria came through seed, Hall Farms alleged Petoseed knew or should have known its source fields were infected. That remained an allegation, not an established knowing sale.

sections.title: Warranty and tort theories followed different appellate paths
paragraphs: Hall Farms sued both sellers for express and implied warranty, negligence, and strict liability. The trial court denied summary judgment. On interlocutory appeal, the Court of Appeals directed judgment on most claims, preserving strict liability against Petoseed and one express warranty against Rispens, and treated both seed-price caps as effective in contract and tort.

Hall Farms sought transfer to restore the broader trial ruling. Justice Krahulik’s Supreme Court majority examined each theory separately rather than making crop loss automatically actionable in all of them.

sections.title: Written performance promises left factual warranty disputes
sections.cue: Explain what language counted and what remained open.
paragraphs: Under Uniform Commercial Code Article 2, whether entirely written statements created warranties was for the court. Factual affirmations and promises could do so without formal labels; praise alone could not. Petoseed’s top-quality description was puffery, but its promise of high vitality, vigor, and germination described performance. Germination and initial growth did not conclusively establish compliance where disease allegedly impaired natural growth and survival. Breach remained factual.

Rispens promised seed properly fitted for seeding, referring to screening and removal of distinguishable foreign seed. Both sides accepted a warranty but disputed whether it covered only identity or latent disease. Ambiguity required factual interpretation. Strictly high-grade seeds also required inquiry into industry meaning, which might concern disease freedom or mere commendation. Rispens as movant had not negated material issues; the intermediate court improperly shifted that burden to Hall Farms. Express-warranty claims against both defendants survived without making every favorable adjective binding.

sections.title: Merchantability depended on the disclaimer and knowledge of usage
sections.cue: Distinguish seed selling from growing crops.
paragraphs: Hall Farms did not challenge on transfer the earlier ruling that Petoseed’s label excluded implied warranties; the majority also noted lack of privity under then-existing Indiana law. Rispens’s written disclaimer, however, omitted merchantability, was inconspicuous, and appeared on an unsigned reverse side, failing written-disclaimer requirements.

Trade usage could still modify or exclude the warranty without invariably requiring actual knowledge. It could bind those in the relevant trade or those who knew or should know it. But Rispens sold seed while Hall Farms planted it and grew crops. Proof of seed merchants’ custom alone did not establish the farmer’s awareness.

Affidavits, including one from the American Seed Trade Association’s executive vice-president, described uniform disclaimer practice, which Hall Farms did not contradict. Other sellers’ purchase orders used similar language, but Mark Hall said he had never read such disclaimers. Whether the farm should be charged with knowledge remained disputed. The court neither rejected the usage’s existence nor made actual reading always necessary.

sections.title: A price cap could allocate risk but still needed assent
sections.cue: Separate validity in principle from this buyer’s agreement.
paragraphs: Both sellers purported to cap damages at the purchase price; Petoseed also excluded incidental and consequential loss across legal theories. The majority held that crop loss exceeding seed price and a latent defect did not make that monetary cap fail its essential purpose: limiting exposure was precisely its purpose. That differed from an exclusive repair remedy unable to restore performance. Latency alone likewise did not make allocation unconscionable. Knowingly supplying defective goods while hiding knowledge would be different, but this record did not conclusively establish such knowledge.

Assent remained unsettled. Mark Hall read the can’s top warranty but not the side limitation, and had not read Rispens’s unsigned reverse-side restriction. Those circumstances left factual questions about mutual agreement. Rejecting the automatic essential-purpose and unconscionability arguments therefore did not finally enforce the caps.

sections.title: The majority placed this gradual product loss outside tort recovery
sections.cue: Give the statutory reasoning and reserved issues.
paragraphs: The historical Indiana strict-liability statute covered sudden, major property damage but excluded gradually developing damage and resulting economic loss. The majority viewed the disease’s development over months as gradual rather than sudden and calamitous, and considered the crop loss damage to the product itself suitable for warranty. Both defendants received judgment on strict liability. It nevertheless rejected an alternative suggestion that a distributor escaped merely because fault concerned the manufacturer; indemnity would follow liability where appropriate.

Petoseed also received negligence judgment because inferior product performance generated economic loss. Warranty rules allocated commercial risk, and negligence could not bypass their negotiated limits. Personal injury or physical damage to other property remained distinct. Hall Farms had not sought transfer of the earlier negligence judgment for Rispens.
With tort claims disposed of, the court reserved whether contract terms could limit tort recovery and did not decide evidence-authentication disputes.

sections.title: Dickson would leave the transmission question for a factfinder
sections.cue: State the partial dissent and exact surviving claims.
paragraphs: Justice Dickson disputed strict-liability dismissal. The record did not establish whether all seed was infected, whether other seed’s produce suffered, or how transmission occurred. A factfinder could decide whether infection spreading to healthy plants or seed caused sudden, major harm. Nor was a cultivated crop merely the purchased seed: it incorporated care, nutrients, and the farm’s growing process. He concurred otherwise.

On September 22, 1993, Krahulik, joined by Chief Justice Shepard and Justices DeBruler and Givan, granted transfer and vacated the Court of Appeals opinion. Remand required summary judgment on all claims except express warranties against both defendants and merchantability against Rispens. Those issues continued without a finding of breach or a crop-damages award.
